sources.quote: According to a Texas Tribune analysis, only 3.6 percent of the lobbyist disclosures for categories that can be itemized if thresholds are met — including food, booze, gifts and entertainment — had any detailed disclosures in 2011.
sources.searcher_note: Tribune's own analysis of Texas lobby reports: itemized (named) share fell from 5.18% in 2005 to 3.6% in 2011; pools gifts with food, drink and entertainment, not gifts alone, and no $1,000+ cut

sources.quote: So when the Texas Ethics Commission increased the per diem, it had the effect of raising the amount lobbyists can spend without providing any details, from $90 to $114, or 60 percent of $190.
sources.searcher_note: Shows the itemization threshold is tied to the per diem and rose in Feb 2015 ($90 to $114); bears on the lead's own caveat that a threshold change, not hiding, could explain a drop; also repeats the 3.6% vs 5.18% figure

sources.outlet: Governing (republished from The Texas Tribune, Ross Ramsey)
sources.quote: More than 95 percent of the money spent by lobbyists during the last decade on food and beverages for state officials and their employees was reported — legally — without naming the recipients of those repasts.
sources.searcher_note: Texas Ethics Commission staff analysis over 2005-2014: named-recipient reports never reached 5% of food and beverage spending; food/drink measure, not gifts

sources.quote: Five ways Texas lobbying laws keep the public in the dark
sources.searcher_note: Page would not load for WebFetch (site error, likely bot wall); search snippet said lobbyists spent nearly $2M on meals in 2021 and named who was at the table less than 2% of the time. Quote is the headline only

sources.quote: The per diem amount is also linked to the amount lobbyists are permitted to spend on gifts to lawmakers without being required to identify the recipient lawmaker by name.
sources.searcher_note: Post-cutoff. TEC proposal to raise per diem $221 to $290.40, lifting the no-name threshold from $132.60 to $174.24 a day; explains the rule, gives no named-share statistics

notes: No source found with the lead's exact measure (reports with $1,000+ in gifts naming a recipient, 61/228 in 2005-11 vs 9/243 since 2019) or the 2012 drop or the 15-filer panel. Closest: Texas Tribune 2013 analysis of the same Texas lobby reports showing named-detail share falling 5.18% (2005) to 3.6% (2011) across food, drink, gifts and entertainment combined. Other sources measure food/beverage only. The Tribune 2015 piece documents a threshold rise in 2015 (tied to per diem), not 2012; no source found on a 2012 threshold change. Some WebSearch calls appeared to run extra internal searches (the TPJ query returned four result sets); logged here as issued.
